title: Chip Alternative — Photonic Computing
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. Photonic computing processes information with light instead of electrons: lasers, waveguides, modulators, and photodetectors replace transistors and copper traces. Advantages: light moves fast with far less heat, many wavelengths can travel one waveguide in parallel (wavelength-division multiplexing), and matrix multiplication — the heart of AI workloads — maps naturally onto optical interference. Challenges: light is hard to store (no good optical memory), components are larger than transistors, and converting between optical and electronic domains costs energy. Status: real research hardware and early commercial optical AI accelerators exist; general-purpose optical CPUs do not. Key players and labs publish steady progress on integrated silicon photonics.

title: Chip Alternative — Spintronic Computing
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. Spintronics uses the electron's spin — not just its charge — to store and process data. Magnetic tunnel junctions (the basis of MRAM memory) already ship in real products: non-volatile, fast, and durable. Research extends spin into logic: spin waves (magnons) can carry signals with very little energy, and spin-based neurons mimic brain-like computing. Advantages: non-volatility (memory that survives power-off), low switching energy, radiation hardness. Challenges: spin signals are weak and hard to route over distance; full spin logic is still laboratory work. Status: MRAM is commercial; spin logic remains research.

title: Chip Alternative — DNA and Biological Computing
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. DNA computing stores data in synthesized DNA strands — a gram of DNA can theoretically hold hundreds of petabytes — and performs computation through biochemical reactions. Real demonstrations: DNA data storage with successful read-back, DNA logic gates, and molecular classifiers that detect disease patterns. Advantages: extreme density, tiny energy per operation, longevity (DNA survives millennia). Challenges: writing DNA is slow and expensive, reading requires sequencing, and reaction times are minutes to hours, not nanoseconds. Status: storage demos are real; general DNA computers are not. Related: protein and cellular computing research.

title: Chip Alternative — Quantum Computing
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. Quantum computers use qubits — quantum bits that can be in superposition — to run algorithms impossible for classical machines, like factoring (Shor's algorithm) and quantum simulation. Real hardware exists from multiple companies and labs: superconducting qubits, trapped ions, photonic qubits, neutral atoms. Advantages: exponential speedups for specific problems. Challenges: qubits are fragile (decoherence), error correction needs many physical qubits per logical qubit, and most everyday computing gains nothing from quantum. Status: noisy intermediate-scale devices are real; fault-tolerant quantum computers are still future. Not a silicon replacement — a specialist accelerator.

title: Chip Alternative — Neuromorphic and Analog Computing
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. Neuromorphic chips mimic brain architecture: neurons and synapses in silicon (or other substrates) that compute with spikes instead of clocked digital logic. Analog computing more broadly does math with continuous physical quantities — voltages, currents, light intensity — instead of digital bits. Advantages: extreme energy efficiency for AI and pattern tasks (orders of magnitude less power), natural parallelism. Challenges: analog is noisy and less precise; programming models are immature; precision-hungry tasks still need digital. Status: real neuromorphic research chips exist (academic and industry labs); analog AI accelerators are entering early commercial use.

title: Chip Alternative — Plasma Computing Substrates
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. Plasma — ionized gas — has been proposed as a computing substrate: plasma waves can carry signals, and plasma antennas already reconfigure by turning plasma elements on and off. Research explores plasma for signal processing and reconfigurable RF systems. Advantages: reconfigurability (turn elements on/off), no solid wear parts. Challenges: containing plasma takes energy and hardware, precision control is hard, and it competes with mature solid-state electronics. Status: plasma antennas are real products; general plasma computing remains research. Note: Manon's item-146 air/plasma computer ecosystem databases are built as a separate lane.

title: Chip Alternative — Superconducting Computing
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. Superconducting logic (single-flux-quantum families) switches with essentially no resistance at cryogenic temperatures, reaching clock speeds far beyond silicon with tiny energy per operation. Advantages: extreme speed and efficiency. Challenges: needs cooling near absolute zero, memory is hard, and the fabrication ecosystem is tiny compared to CMOS. Status: real laboratory processors exist; no commercial general-purpose superconducting CPU. Often paired with quantum computers as control electronics.

title: Chip Alternative — Other Alternative Substrates
body: Public edition. Public technology reference, fact-checked. More alternatives to silicon chips: carbon nanotube transistors (real prototype processors built), memristors (resistors with memory, for in-memory computing), optical/photonic interconnects, spintronic memory covered separately, diamond and silicon-carbide for extreme environments, and mechanical computing (modern micro-mechanical logic for radiation-hard niches). Each trades something: density, speed, energy, or environment tolerance. No single substrate beats silicon CMOS at everything — alternatives win in niches and may combine into hybrid systems.
